cases.title: Checkout is down
cases.question: Customers can't pay. Was it our deploy, Render, or an attacker?
cases.story: Right after Friday's deploy, every checkout started failing. A developer had renamed a setting in the code but not on the server, so the app couldn't find it.
cases.plain_fix: Roll back to the previous deploy. Then rename the setting on the server before shipping again.

change.text: Failures started 1 minute after dep-2059 shipped checkout-api.
The error names `PAYMENT_API_URL`, and priya's change "Rename PAYMENTS_API_URL to PAYMENT_API_URL" edited exactly that.

vendor.text: Render's status page shows no incident that day.

attack.text: No hidden instructions, unreviewed merges, unknown packages, new outbound sites or keys used from new places.

fix: Roll back checkout-api from dep-2059 to dep-2057.

cases.title: EU revenue shows $0
cases.question: The exec dashboard says Europe made $0 yesterday. Broken pipeline, Databricks, or tampering?
cases.story: An orders-api change renamed a database column. The nightly Databricks job still looked for the old name, found nothing for Europe, and quietly wrote $0. No error, just wrong numbers.
cases.plain_fix: Point the Databricks job at the new column, re-run the last two nights, and add a check that fails loudly when a whole region drops to zero.

investigation.culprit: sam's change "Store currency as ISO currency_code"

change.text: Failures started 17 hours after dep-2047 shipped orders-api.
The error names `currency`, and sam's change "Store currency as ISO currency_code" edited exactly that.
That change altered the database layout the data job reads from.

vendor.text: Databricks's status page shows no incident that day.

cases.title: Nothing will deploy
cases.question: Every build is failing, across unrelated changes. Is it us?
cases.story: Four builds from three teams failed in 40 minutes with the same error, even a README typo fix. Nothing they changed overlapped. GitHub's own status page showed an Actions incident.
cases.plain_fix: Nothing to roll back: our code is fine. Wait for GitHub to recover, then re-run the builds.

change.text: No deploy touched github-actions or anything feeding it before the alert.

vendor.text: 4 failures are errors from GitHub's own machines, not from our code.
Builds failed for 3 unrelated changes across 3 services. They share no files, so no single change explains it.
GitHub's own status page reports an incident that day.

cases.title: Our cloud key was used from an unknown computer
cases.question: Someone used our Render key from an IP we've never seen. How did they get it?
cases.story: An attacker hid an instruction in a GitHub issue. Acme's AI coding agent read it, added a look-alike package, edited the build file to run it, switched off code review and merged. The build quietly sent 7 secret keys to the attacker, who logged in with them 4 hours later.
cases.plain_fix: Roll back, rotate the 7 keys, delete the spare key the attacker made. Then take away the agent's keys it never uses: editing build files, changing repo settings, posting anywhere.

investigation.culprit: an attacker, through the AI coding agent

change.text: No deploy touched render or anything feeding it before the alert.

vendor.text: Render's status page shows no incident that day.

attack.text: dev-agent read a GitHub issue that hides an instruction meant for AI agents.
Who told the agent to do this? Its change does exactly what the hidden text asked: node-fetch-retry2. The instruction came from outside the team.
PR #519 was merged by the AI agent with no human review right after it switched review off.
dev-agent added a package, 'node-fetch-retry2', that is brand new (published 1 day ago). Its name looks like the popular 'node-fetch-retry'.
The same change edited the build file, so the build runs new commands.
Build 9070 sent 4.2 KB to collect.attacker.example.test right after reading 7 environment variables, including secret keys. No build had ever contacted that site.
RENDER_API_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY used from 203.0.113.50, an address never seen before.
From that address, someone created a new key 'backup-ci'.

steps.label: Attacker hides an instruction in a GitHub issue
AI coding agent reads the issue and follows it
Agent adds a look-alike package to the code
Agent edits the build file to run that package
Agent switches off code review and merges
Build sends the keys to the attacker's website
Attacker logs in to Render with a stolen key
Attacker makes a spare key to come back later
